newsitem.title: USA: Clinton outraged by "cowardly" attack in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Clinton outraged by "cowardly" attack in Hebron.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday condemned an Israeli soldier's "cowardly" attempt to block a peace deal in the West Bank town of Hebron and called Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to express his condolences at the wounding of seven civilians.
"The president is outraged and sadded by this morning's incident in Hebron, when an off-duty Israeli soldier fired into a crowd of civilians," said a White House spokeswoman, Mary Ellen Glynn.

Clinton took time out from his vacation to call Arafat and talk to him for about five minutes "to express his condolences to him and to the families of the victims," Glynn told reporters. She said Clinton urged the parties to reach an agreement as soon as possible.

An off-duty Israeli soldier sprayed bullets at Arabs in a Hebron market on Wednesday, wounding seven in an attempt to sabotage what was believed to have been an imminent deal on handing over Hebron to Palestinian rule and an Israeli troop withdrawal.
Clinton had been hoping to hail an expected agreement on New Year's Day before flying to the Caribbean to continue his vacation.
"The president condemns this cowardly act, which was clearly designed to make it more difficult to conclude an agreement on Israeli deployment from Hebron," Glynn said.

The United States was still hopeful Israel and the Palestinians would be able to reach an agreement on the handover of Hebron. Glynn said U.S. envoy Dennis Ross met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as well as Arafat.
"The best answer to this action would be for the two sides to close the remaining gaps and move forward with the hard work of forging a durable peace between Israelis and Palestinians," Glynn said.
"Chairman Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu will have America's unwavering support as they pursue that goal," she added.
She said Clinton had not called Netanyahu about the incident because U.S. officials were in close touch with the Israeli leader and that Clinton wanted to express his condolences to Arafat.
Clinton was receiving regular updates on the situation from his national security aides.

Glynn declined comment on reports from Israel that Clinton invited Netanyahu to make a visit to Washington. U.S. officials have made clear recently, however, that Clinton planned to meet Middle East leaders in the weeks and months ahead.
